site_article.headline: Gemini now lets users preview and edit the files it creates inside the chat
site_article.dek: Documents, PDFs, spreadsheets, slide decks and code can be revised without downloading them first, though phones support only PDFs for now.
site_article.summary: Google announced on October 29, 2026 that the Gemini app can preview and edit the files it generates directly in the conversation. The feature is available to all users, with PDF editing on web and mobile and other formats on the web only.
site_article.seo_title: Gemini adds in-chat editing for documents, PDFs and sheets
site_article.seo_description: Google's Gemini app can now preview and edit the documents, PDFs, spreadsheets and code it creates, inside the chat. PDFs work on mobile; the rest is web only.
site_article.answer_summary: Yes. Since October 29, 2026, Gemini can open the files it creates in the chat and let users edit them by hand or by asking Gemini for changes. On phones, only PDFs can be edited so far.
site_article.hero_alt: A smartphone showing the Gemini app on its screen.

paragraphs.text: Google announced on October 29, 2026 that users of the Gemini app can now generate, preview and edit documents, PDFs, presentations, spreadsheets and code directly inside a chat, according to Digital Trends and Chrome Geek.

Gemini gained the ability to create downloadable files earlier this year, in April. Until now, though, a file with an error had to be opened in another app or regenerated from scratch, Chrome Geek reported. With the update, files Gemini creates open in the conversation, so users can check them before downloading.

There are three ways to change a file. Users can expand it to a full screen view and type changes by hand, highlight a passage and ask Gemini a question about it, or ask Gemini in the chat to revise the file. Digital Trends reported that highlighted sections can also be rewritten or have their visuals changed on request.

Thurrott described the same flow: a user can open a generated document in full screen, edit it manually, then return to the conversation and ask Gemini for another round of changes. The preview window also has an Export button for saving the finished file, according to Chrome Geek.

Google's own example is aimed at students. In its demo, photos of handwritten lecture notes are turned into a PDF study guide, which opens in the chat, can be edited and refined section by section, and can be questioned further without leaving the conversation.
Where it works and who gets it

Support depends on the device. Digital Trends and Chrome Geek reported that PDF preview and editing work on both the web and the Gemini mobile app, while Google Docs, Google Sheets, slide decks, Markdown, plain text files and code can currently be edited only in the web app. Chromebook users who open gemini.google.com get the web version with every format.

Google said the features are available to all users in every language and region where the Gemini app is offered. Neither report mentioned a paid plan requirement, and Thurrott described the editing tools as available now, without a staged rollout.

The update arrives during a busy month for Gemini. Gemini 4 Argon reached AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app earlier in October, and Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, a model built for cybersecurity work, on October 28, according to Thurrott and Digital Trends.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the change matters more than its size suggests. Chat assistants have been good at drafting but awkward at the last step, where a document needs small fixes before it is usable. Keeping that step inside the conversation removes a round trip to another app and makes Gemini a more direct competitor to the document tools people already use. The mobile limit is the clear gap: most formats still need a computer, so the phone experience is mainly about PDFs for now.

The next thing to watch is whether Google brings Docs, Sheets and slide deck editing to the Gemini mobile app, which would make the feature useful for the many people who work mostly from their phones.
